strengths: The paper presents a coherent and practically useful extension of 3DGS representation learning: complementary language-aligned, generalist, and object-aware 2D teachers supervise one feed-forward scene encoder through teacher-specific projectors.

The empirical coverage is unusually broad. Results include four open-vocabulary semantic benchmarks, ScanNet200 instance segmentation, five probing/fine-tuning benchmarks, data-scarce settings, and two language-based tasks. Several improvements are substantial, including ScanNet200 linear probing (36.0 versus 28.8 mIoU for Sonata), ScanNet++ linear probing (48.8 versus 40.7), and ScanNet200 tail-class instance AP (13.0 versus 5.4 for Mosaic3D).

The point-cloud-compatible variant is a useful finding: a model pretrained from Gaussian-derived centers, colors, and normals transfers strongly to conventional point-cloud benchmarks despite the representation mismatch.
The paper includes useful analyses of individual design choices, scaling, noise robustness, model size, inference time, and adaptation storage. These go beyond reporting only final benchmark values.
The render-and-distill formulation is appealing in practice because it avoids storing uplifted per-Gaussian teacher features, while retaining differentiable image-plane supervision.
weaknesses: The supervision protocol is insufficiently transparent and potentially confounds several central comparisons. Equation 6 optionally uses ground-truth semantic and instance labels for contrastive pretraining, but the manuscript does not clearly identify which main checkpoints use these losses or on which datasets. If ScanNet-family labels enter pretraining, comparisons against self-supervised Sonata and claims about zero-shot transfer and data efficiency require careful qualification and label-budget accounting.

The evidence for teacher complementarity is incomplete. Table 9 only adds teachers sequentially and omits DINO-only, PE-only, language+PE, and matched-compute controls. PE adds only 0.2 mIoU on the in-domain split in this table. No repeated-run uncertainty is reported, so the significance of small gains is unclear.

The adaptation claims are stronger than the supporting comparison. Table 7 reports preprocessing and storage but not total training time, repeated online teacher-inference cost, or peak compute. Effectiveness is shown as a 2.7-point gain over the unadapted model, without a matched offline-uplifting adaptation baseline. Thus, reduced storage is demonstrated, but overall acceleration or superiority is not.

Reproducibility is limited in the provided manuscript. Exact contrastive equations, augmentation equations, camera-selection thresholds, training schedules, and further ablations are deferred to an unavailable supplement; code is only promised. The new InteriorGS benchmark construction, label mapping, splits, and evaluation protocol also receive little description.

The novelty is meaningful but incremental: the central method combines SceneSplat's lift-then-align pipeline with established multi-teacher distillation and per-teacher projectors. The paper does not directly establish that the shared latent space integrates the teachers rather than allocating separate subspaces that the projectors decode.

Some conclusions are overstated or internally unclear. VQA does not improve consistently—ScanQA METEOR falls from 22.9 to 22.5—and several point-cloud probing rows trail Sonata. The claimed broad native-3DGS capability is partly supported through a separately pretrained point-cloud-input variant rather than the full Gaussian-parameter encoder. Absolute pretraining-scene counts and the bases for the reported 8.32× and 39.9× data reductions should also be stated consistently.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant, underexplored problem: learning transferable scene-level representations directly from 3D Gaussian primitives. Combining language-aligned, generalist, and spatially aware 2D teachers is sensible and potentially useful.

The empirical scope is unusually broad, covering open-vocabulary semantic and instance segmentation, probing, finetuning, low-data learning, domain adaptation, and VQA across several indoor-scene datasets.

Several reported improvements are substantial. For example, Chorus raises ScanNet200 linear-probing mIoU from Sonata's 28.8 to 36.0 and improves zero-shot InteriorGS f-mIoU from SceneSplat's 10.1 to 15.7 under joint-dataset training.

The point-cloud-compatible variant is practically interesting, and the paper reports model size, inference time, preprocessing/storage costs, and some transfer analyses rather than presenting benchmark accuracy alone.

The manuscript is generally well organized and the main architecture and motivation are easy to follow. weaknesses: The central evaluation protocol is insufficiently specified and potentially confounds the claimed zero-shot and data-efficiency conclusions. Equation 6 includes semantic- and instance-label contrastive losses, while Table 1 evaluates on validation sets from datasets also listed as pretraining sources. The manuscript does not clearly state which labels were used for every main model or how class overlap was controlled. Consequently, it is unclear whether gains arise from holistic teacher distillation, target-dataset label supervision, or both.

The comparison with Sonata is not supervision-matched. Sonata is self-supervised, whereas Chorus distills three very large pretrained 2D models and may additionally use semantic and instance annotations. Comparing only the number of 3D training scenes—and emphasizing 39.9x fewer scenes—ignores the much stronger external supervision, rendered views, and pseudo-label computation available to Chorus.

The principal novelty is incremental relative to SceneSplat and existing multi-teacher distillation: a shared encoder, teacher-specific MLP heads, PHI-S normalization, and summed matching losses. The proposed 3DGS augmentations and render-and-distill adaptation could strengthen the contribution, but their defining equations and essential implementation details are deferred to an unavailable supplement, preventing technical assessment and reproduction from the submitted manuscript.

The ablations do not isolate the claimed cause of improvement adequately. Teachers are added cumulatively, without compute-matched single-teacher controls, independent DINO/PE experiments, or tests separating additional supervision from teacher complementarity. Likewise, the robustness experiment covers only 684 instances from ten scenes and does not establish the proposed explanation for point-cloud transfer.

The adaptation efficiency comparison is incomplete. Table 7 reports rasterization as the online overhead but the method also requires online inference through multiple large 2D teachers. It omits total training time, accelerator usage, and teacher-inference cost, so the claimed efficiency advantage over precomputed features is not supported by the presented accounting.

Several claims overstate or contradict the tables. The paper says VQA improves consistently, but ScanQA METEOR decreases from 22.9 to 22.5. It cites 50.2 mIoU on ScanNet++, whereas Table 4 reports 52.9, and describes a 4.5-point low-label gain as mAP although Table 5 reports semantic-segmentation scores. Similar probing results are mixed rather than uniformly superior.

No repeated-run variation, confidence intervals, or significance analysis is reported. This matters for small gains such as 0.3–0.8 points, especially given that teacher choice, pseudo-label generation, and finetuning can introduce substantial variance.

Reproducibility is weak: absolute pretraining scene counts and dataset composition are obscured by relative multipliers; training schedules, batch sizes, sampling, optimizer details, projector dimensions, validity masks, augmentation formulas, decoder configurations, and benchmark construction/splits for the per-Gaussian InteriorGS evaluation are missing. Code and models are only promised after publication.

Overall, the paper has worthwhile empirical ideas and promising results, but unclear supervision fairness, incomplete cost accounting, limited causal ablation, and missing core methodological details materially weaken the evidence for its strongest claims. These are substantive scientific concerns rather than presentation-only refinements.

strengths: Chorus addresses a timely and underexplored problem: learning a feed-forward, general-purpose encoder directly over 3D Gaussian scene primitives, rather than attaching task-specific features to individual scenes.

The shared encoder with teacher-specific projectors is technically coherent, and combining language-aligned SigLIP2, generalist DINOv3, and spatially localized PE-Spatial supervision is well motivated. PHI-S standardization and staged teacher introduction are sensible mechanisms for handling heterogeneous teachers.

The evaluation is unusually broad, covering open-vocabulary semantic and instance segmentation, linear and decoder probing, full finetuning, low-data learning, point-cloud transfer, and 3D question answering across several datasets. Results are generally strong: for example, joint-training gains over SceneSplat include 3.2 foreground mIoU on ScanNet200 and 5.6 on InteriorGS, while point-cloud probing substantially improves over Sonata on ScanNet200 and ScanNet++.

The paper provides useful evidence beyond headline accuracy. Teacher and design-choice ablations support the main components; the noisy-point-cloud retrieval experiment probes the proposed robustness explanation; and the storage, runtime, parameter-count, and adaptation-resolution analyses expose practical tradeoffs.

The render-and-distill adaptation mechanism is practically appealing: it uses 3DGS rendering to avoid storing roughly 1 TB of uplifted teacher features in the reported InteriorGS setting. The 2.7 mIoU adaptation gain with 100 scenes suggests that this is more than an engineering convenience.

The manuscript is clear and well organized, with effective overview figures and readable tables. The contribution is somewhat incremental conceptually, but its integration, empirical scope, and demonstrated usefulness form a sufficiently strong case for acceptance.
weaknesses: The central comparison against self-supervised point-cloud pretraining is not fully controlled. Chorus uses powerful 2D teachers and also employs semantic- and instance-label-based contrastive losses when labels are available, whereas Sonata is self-supervised. Consequently, the reported 39.9-fold scene-efficiency advantage cannot be attributed specifically to 3DGS pretraining or the proposed multi-teacher architecture; it also reflects substantially richer supervision. This supervision should be foregrounded when interpreting the data-efficiency and transfer claims.

The teacher ablation is incomplete. The paper shows language-only, language+DINO, and language+DINO+PE configurations, but not DINO-only, PE-only, language+PE, or matched single-teacher baselines under the same data and schedule. Some rows also change the training source. Thus, the evidence establishes incremental gains for one addition order but does not fully substantiate the claimed complementarity or disentangle teacher choice from extra objectives and training stages.

Several claims are overstated or internally inconsistent. The VQA replacement does not improve every metric—ScanQA METEOR decreases from 22.9 to 22.5—despite the claim of consistent improvement. The text reports 50.2 mIoU on ScanNet++, whereas Table 4 reports 52.9, and the low-label gain is called +4.5 mAP although Table 5 reports semantic mIoU. These appear correctable, but they reduce confidence in the quantitative presentation.

Important reproducibility details are deferred to a supplement not included in the provided manuscript. In particular, the exact 3DGS-aware augmentation equations and strengths, contrastive formulation, teacher start epochs, optimizer and batch schedule, pseudo-label validity rules, projector dimensions, and view-selection thresholds are absent. Since several of these choices drive the ablations, the current main manuscript and promise of future code release are insufficient for close reproduction.

The proposed rendering-equivalent and immature-manifold augmentations are potentially original, but the manuscript gives only qualitative descriptions and an aggregated design ablation. It does not measure rendering equivalence, isolate the two augmentations, or compare them individually against matched conventional perturbations, so their specific technical contribution remains weakly supported.

Most experiments concern indoor scenes derived from closely related RGB-D datasets, and the adaptation study reports only linear probing on InteriorGS. Evidence for robustness to substantially different environments, outdoor scenes, or independently generated 3DGS pipelines is therefore limited. Runtime is also higher than all listed baselines, and training or teacher-feature extraction cost is not comprehensively reported.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and relatively underexplored problem: learning a feed-forward, reusable scene representation directly from 3D Gaussian primitives. Combining language-aligned, generalist, and object-aware 2D teachers through a shared backbone and teacher-specific projectors is sensible and moderately original in the 3DGS setting.

The empirical study is unusually broad. It covers zero-shot semantic and instance segmentation, linear and decoder probing, full finetuning, limited-supervision settings, VQA, out-of-domain adaptation, and both native 3DGS and point-cloud inputs across several datasets.

Several improvements are substantial. Examples include ScanNet200 zero-shot f-mIoU increasing from 22.5 for the retrained SceneSplat baseline to 24.6, InteriorGS from 10.0 to 15.7, ScanNet200 linear-probe mIoU from 28.8 for Sonata to 36.0, and stronger tail-class open-vocabulary instance segmentation. Robustness tests across Gaussian density, reconstruction algorithms, and iPhone point clouds add useful evidence.

The paper includes relevant component ablations, including incremental teachers, regression losses, staging, contrastive supervision, 3DGS-aware augmentation, teacher resolution, and adaptation-set size. It also reports model size, inference time, preprocessing time, and storage costs.
The manuscript is generally well organized, and the supplementary material provides useful detail about uplifting, the InteriorGS benchmark construction, adaptation, and downstream protocols.
weaknesses: The comparison to self-supervised point-cloud pretraining is not fully controlled. Chorus uses outputs from very large externally pretrained 2D foundation models and also uses semantic-class and instance labels in its contrastive pretraining losses, while Sonata is self-supervised. Consequently, claims that multi-teacher pretraining is more data-efficient based on counting only 3D scenes—especially the emphasized 39.9x figure—do not account for teacher training data, teacher inference cost, source annotations, or model capacity (Chorus has 131.3M parameters versus Sonata's 108.5M). The limited-annotation results are also difficult to interpret as annotation efficiency when source-dataset labels were already used during pretraining.

The evidence isolating the central multi-teacher contribution is incomplete. The main incremental ablation primarily measures zero-shot semantic segmentation; it does not establish how each teacher affects instance segmentation, VQA, point-cloud transfer, or data efficiency. PE-Spatial adds only 0.2 f-mIoU on the ScanNet++ validation setting in Table 9, and in supplementary Table C it reduces decoder-probe mIoU from 28.9 to 28.3. Capacity-matched single-teacher and alternative multi-teacher aggregation baselines are absent.

The claimed broadly applicable annotation-free adaptation procedure relies, in its demonstrated implementation, on InteriorGS occupancy maps and a label-guided camera-height heuristic that explicitly queries furniture, floor, and ceiling labels. Moreover, adaptation is evaluated mainly through a linear-probing gain, without a quality comparison against offline uplifting or an end-to-end timing/accuracy tradeoff. This materially weakens the claims that it readily adapts to new domains without expensive preprocessing or 3D annotations.

The rendering-equivalent augmentation is not technically well justified. Equation 13 samples displacement as Sigma times a standard Gaussian, yielding covariance proportional to Sigma squared and dimensionally producing squared-length displacement if Sigma is a spatial covariance; a covariance-square-root factor would normally be expected. Vanishing first-order change only preserves rendered color in expectation locally, not individual renderings under nonlinear projection, visibility, and compositing. No rendered-image PSNR or other measurement verifies the asserted approximate rendering equivalence.

Reproducibility is limited despite the extensive supplement. Important pretraining details are missing or insufficiently precise, including optimizer and learning-rate schedule, batch construction, total epochs, exact teacher activation and warm-up epochs, validity-mask thresholds, augmentation probabilities and magnitudes such as eta and beta, and several open-vocabulary inference details. The manuscript's statement that code is released does not substitute for a self-contained specification.

Some conclusions are overstated relative to the evidence. The VQA replacement does not improve every metric—ScanQA METEOR decreases from 22.9 to 22.5—and the generally modest differences are reported without variation across runs. The newly generated InteriorGS Gaussian labels rely on bounding-box and largest-connected-component heuristics, but their accuracy is not manually validated, making fine-grained conclusions on that benchmark less secure.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and underexplored problem: learning reusable feed-forward scene representations directly from 3D Gaussian primitives rather than attaching features to each scene through per-scene optimization.

The empirical scope is unusually broad. Chorus is evaluated on open-vocabulary semantic and instance segmentation, semantic and instance probing, low-data transfer, VQA, domain adaptation, and both 3DGS and point-cloud inputs across several datasets.

Many results are quantitatively strong. For example, joint-data zero-shot segmentation improves over SceneSplat from 22.5 to 24.6 f-mIoU on ScanNet200, 14.0 to 18.7 on Matterport3D, and 10.0 to 15.7 on InteriorGS. Linear probing also improves substantially over Sonata on ScanNet200 and ScanNet++.

The paper includes useful analyses beyond headline benchmarks: teacher and design ablations, robustness to Gaussian density and optimization method, iPhone RGB-D inputs, noisy-point retrieval, runtime/model size, and qualitative feature visualizations.

The render-and-distill adaptation idea is practically motivated, substantially reducing reported preprocessing and storage costs relative to offline uplifting. The supplementary material gives a reasonably concrete algorithm and explains the view-selection pipeline.
The manuscript is generally clear and well organized, and the shared-backbone/per-teacher-projector formulation is technically plausible.
weaknesses: The central attribution to multi-teacher learning is not fully isolated. Relative to SceneSplat, Chorus simultaneously changes teachers, feature standardization, contrastive supervision, augmentations, staging, model capacity, and part of the training data processing. The ablations show incremental gains but do not provide a controlled comparison against equally strong single-teacher models under matched capacity and compute, nor against a simple ensemble or concatenation baseline.

The advertised data-efficiency factors based on training-scene counts are potentially misleading. Chorus receives supervision from large 2D foundation models and also uses semantic- and instance-label-derived contrastive losses when labels are available, whereas Sonata is self-supervised. Scene count alone therefore does not establish sample or compute efficiency, and teacher pretraining data and offline pseudo-label generation costs are excluded.

The adaptation claims are broader than the evidence. Performance is demonstrated only on InteriorGS, with no comparison of final accuracy against offline uplifting. Moreover, the pose-generation procedure uses InteriorGS occupancy maps and nearby semantic labels to choose camera height, so the claim that adaptation can operate conveniently on new data without provided poses or costly 3D information is not validated in a label-free setting.

Some narrative claims overstate the tables. Chorus does not improve every linear-probing metric over Sonata—for example, Matterport3D mAcc is 25.7 versus 25.8—and its ScanQA METEOR score decreases from 22.9 to 22.5 despite the claim of consistent VQA improvements. The VQA comparison also changes the task-guided sparsifier to a single attention block, so it is not a strict backbone-only swap.

The proposed “rendering-equivalent” augmentation has weak theoretical support. Using Σξ as a position displacement yields covariance Σ² rather than Σ, is dimensionally questionable without specifying the units of its scale, and zero expected first-order change does not demonstrate preservation of rendered appearance. No rendering-error or image-quality measurement validates the claimed equivalence.

InteriorGS labels are generated from bounding boxes using a largest-connected-component heuristic and a manually constructed 755-to-72 class mapping, yet annotation accuracy or sensitivity to these choices is not measured. This weakens conclusions drawn from the newly introduced benchmark.

Important reproducibility details remain missing, including the augmentation magnitudes, teacher activation epochs, full pretraining schedule, batch construction, and total pretraining/teacher-extraction compute. The manuscript also states that code is released but provides no accessible repository in the submitted version.

Overall, these issues weaken causal interpretation and several efficiency/adaptation claims, but they do not erase the consistent gains across many established evaluations. The supported empirical contribution therefore favors weak acceptance rather than rejection.

strengths: Chorus addresses a timely and underexplored problem: learning transferable, feed-forward scene representations directly from 3D Gaussian primitives. Extending SceneSplat from primarily language-aligned features to a shared backbone distilled from language, generalist, and object-aware teachers is technically sensible and useful.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad. It covers zero-shot semantic and instance segmentation, linear and decoder probing, full finetuning, limited-label and limited-scene regimes, VQA, domain adaptation, input-density robustness, and transfer to point clouds across several datasets.

The principal results are strong. For example, joint-data Chorus improves over SceneSplat from 22.5 to 24.6 f-mIoU on ScanNet200, 14.0 to 18.7 on Matterport3D, and 10.0 to 15.7 on the unseen InteriorGS benchmark. Its point-cloud variant also provides large linear-probing gains over Sonata on ScanNet200 and ScanNet++.

The paper provides useful component analysis: adding DINO and PE generally improves transfer, staged PE training performs better than introducing it from the start, and the proposed losses and 3DGS-aware augmentations provide incremental gains. Robustness experiments additionally cover Gaussian density, optimization variants, noisy point clouds, and iPhone RGB-D captures.

The render-and-distill adaptation procedure is practically appealing: it avoids storing roughly 1 TB of uplifted features in the reported setting, and its gain scales with teacher resolution and adaptation data. The manuscript is generally clear, visually polished, and supplemented with algorithmic and dataset-processing details.
weaknesses: The conceptual novelty is moderate. The central recipe combines an existing lift-then-align 3DGS encoder with established multi-teacher distillation, PHI-S normalization, and teacher-specific heads. The paper demonstrates that this combination works well, but does not deeply establish why the shared representation is superior to alternatives such as separate encoders, feature fusion, or a matched-capacity single-teacher model.

The headline scene-efficiency comparisons are not fully controlled. Chorus receives supervision from very large pretrained 2D teachers and sometimes semantic or instance labels through contrastive losses, whereas Sonata is self-supervised. Counting only the number of 3D scenes, while omitting teacher pretraining data, rendered views, pseudo-label generation, storage, and total compute, makes the claimed 39.9x efficiency advantage difficult to interpret.

Several important pretraining details needed for reproduction are missing from the manuscript and supplement, including the total schedule and exact teacher activation epochs, optimizer and learning-rate schedule, batch construction, augmentation probabilities, the value of eta and the beta range in the proposed perturbations, and validity-mask thresholds. Downstream and adaptation settings are described more thoroughly than the core pretraining procedure.

The evaluation has no repeated-run variation or significance estimates. Some conclusions rest on small changes, such as the 0.2 f-mIoU gain from adding PE on the ScanNet++ validation split, while PE slightly reduces decoder-probing mIoU in the supplementary ablation. Broader comparisons with recent related representation learners such as Concerto and GaussTR would also strengthen the state-of-the-art claims.

A few claims overstate the tables. Chorus does not improve every VQA metric: ScanQA METEOR falls from 22.9 to 22.5 despite the statement of consistent improvements. The text also reports 50.2 mIoU for ScanNet++ full finetuning while Table 4 gives 52.9. These appear readily correctable, but should be fixed.
